Are you a mineral owner?

You might be one and not know it.

If you own the oil, gas, or mineral rights under a piece of land — even if you don't own the surface — you're a mineral owner. Many people inherit rights without paperwork in hand: a royalty check, an old division order, or a county tax notice is often the first clue. If any of those sound familiar, your owner record is probably already in the public rolls — and you can claim it free.

Trust promise

Owner-first is a product rule, not a slogan.

Not a broker

Mineral View doesn't buy your minerals, and we don't help buyers pressure you to sell. We surface public records, production, permits, and operator activity so you decide from a stronger position.

Your data is never sold

Owner data isn't sold, brokered, or bundled to third parties. Documents you upload stay private unless you explicitly share them with an advisor — and you can revoke that anytime.

Estimates, not appraisals

Valuation numbers are model-based estimates using public records and stated assumptions. They are not formal appraisals — and every valuation surface is labeled that way.

For professionals

Operators and advisors work here too — on their own data, never yours.

Mineral View is owner-first. Professional accounts are a separate, contact-only product that runs on public and operator records. They never touch owner portfolios, uploads, or personal data.

Operators

Know your footprint — and your neighbors

Your wells, leases, permits, and completions on the live Texas map · RRC filing tracking · publish updates to the owners under your units. Gross/operational data only — never an owner's share.

Advisors & landmen

Run a book of owner clients

Manage many owner clients from one dashboard · white-label weekly reports · delegated, revocable access. You advise a client only with their consent — and are always labeled "representing," never acting as the owner.

How this protects owners. Professional tools never see owner accounts, uploaded documents, or personal data. Owner information is never sold, and no operator or buyer can pay to change what an owner sees. An advisor sees a client's record only after that owner grants access — and the owner can revoke it at any time.

Don't want a subscription?

Buy a single Lease Audit — $500 per audit, once, done.

One lease audited — expected vs paid, month by month, from the statements you send — plus the written plain-English report and a walkthrough call. No subscription, no auto-renew, no surprises. If you later subscribe annual, we credit $100 of it toward your first year.

The arithmetic: three audits bought this way is $1,500. Premium is $999.50 a year and includes those three — plus the daily watch, the weekly report, and the monthly mailed report.

Request a single audit — $500 Mineral View confirms scope and sends an invoice — no card is charged from this page or get 3 audits a year included with a 12-month Premium term

How the 1-year term works

Every paid plan is a 12-month committed term starting at checkout. Pay monthly within the term or prepay the year — two months free vs monthly (annual is exactly 10× the monthly price — Essentials $499.50/yr · Premium $999.50/yr). Payments are processed by Braintree (a PayPal service).

Renewal needs your explicit approval

Paid plans never auto-renew into a new term. We remind you before your end of term; if you do nothing, billing stops and your account moves to Free. Renewing is one explicit click — always your approval, never a surprise charge.

Upgrades are immediate & prorated

Upgrade any time — it takes effect immediately and you're billed only the prorated difference through your existing end of term. Referral credits auto-apply at your next renewal.

Downgrades happen at term end

Downgrades and cancellations take effect at the end of your term — never mid-term. If your next plan shows fewer leases, you pick which leases stay visible before the term ends; everything else is archived, never deleted, and restored in full if you upgrade again.

◆
Referral credits — two tiers: $50 when a referred owner creates a free account + $100 more after they enter and remain in a paid 12-month term past the confirmation window (monthly billing or annual prepay both qualify). Credits are non-cash and apply to your next renewal, upgrade, or eligible service — never a brokerage fee.

Prices in U.S. dollars, exclusive of applicable taxes shown at checkout. Full mechanics in the Subscription Terms · Terms of Use.

Public Q&A · Bee County Ownersasked 3 days ago · 640 views

Operator moved a rig onto my section — should I expect payment soon?

Dawn A. · Martin Co. owner · public groups auto-flag private data — no decimals, dollar amounts, or documents appear here

RB
R. Barnes Top answer

A rig is the start of a long clock, not a check in the mail. Typical Texas timeline: spud → ~90 days to first production → division order to sign → first check 120–180 days after first production (Texas NRC sets a 120-day pay window). So realistically: six months to a year from the day you saw the rig.

TW
T. Whitfield

Watch the permits and completions layers on the free map — the completion filing is your best early signal that the pay clock actually started.

GC
G. Cantu

And when the division order shows up — check the decimal against your deed before signing. The guides here walk through it.

Reading is free for everyone. Answering takes a free account — claiming your record connects you with owners on your leases.

One owner is easy to ignore. A room full of them isn’t.

County, operator and play rooms are free to read — no account needed. A free account lets you post and reply. Claiming your record opens the private room for your own lease, with the people who own it alongside you. Same rooms as on mineralview.com — you just have more to do in them here.

What a group actually does for a mineral owner

The honest answer

Most mineral owners are alone with it: one statement a month, nothing to compare it against, no leverage with the operator, and no realistic way to pay a professional. A group changes all four — not because talking is nice, but because of the arithmetic.

◉ Find out whether you're being paid like everyone else

A single statement is unfalsifiable — there's no second number in it. Owners on the same lease, same month, same volumes, comparing what they were actually paid: that's the only comparison that exists, and it's how underpayment gets found.

◆ Face the operator as a group

One owner with half a percent gets a form letter. Twelve owners of the same unit asking the same question get an answer — a deduction breakdown, a recompletion plan, a corrected division order. Things an individual simply cannot demand.

✚ Hire professionals at a fraction of the cost

A royalty audit is around $5,000. Nobody with a small interest buys that alone. Twelve owners split it to ≈$417 each; twenty to ≈$250. The median shared Texas lease carries 24 owners of record. Fee illustrative; the owner count is measured.

⌲ Share what each of you already knows

Permits next door, offer letters circulating the county, how to read a deduction line, which operators post late. One owner catches a sliver of it. A room of owners sees the pattern.

◆
The short version: an owner with half a percent will never pay for an accountant on their own. Fifty of them together will. That is the whole idea — and on the median shared lease there are twenty-four of you.
MView — Official Account Official · the only seeded voice here

These rooms are new, and we are honest about what that means. Mineral View does not create fake members and never will. The starting posts in every room come from this one clearly marked account, made of data we already hold — new permits on your units, this month’s activity, a price move, how to read a deduction line. Everything else here was written by a real owner.

A platform whose whole argument is “we have no financial interest in your answer” does not get to invent its own audience. A quiet room with real people in it beats a busy one with invented ones.

FAQ

Fair questions, straight answers.

Is Mineral View a broker?
No. We help mineral owners understand public records, activity, monthly production, and estimates so they can make better decisions. We don't buy minerals, we don't sell your information to buyers, and we don't take operator money.
Are your valuations appraisals?
No. Every valuation is a model-based estimate — not a formal appraisal. Every valuation surface is labeled and includes the assumptions used.
Do you sell my data?
No. Owner data is not sold, brokered, or bundled to third parties. Documents you upload are private to you unless you explicitly share them with an advisor — and you can revoke advisor sharing anytime.
What if the public records look wrong?
Use "Report a data issue" anywhere it appears. We review your report and use it to improve your Mineral View record. Public records at the source agency may still need correction with the operator or state — we don't overwrite public records ourselves in v1.
How is Free different from Essentials and Premium?
All three give you 1 active owner. Free is 1 visible lease and the weekly report cut down to the headline plus that lease. Essentials — $49.95/mo is up to 5 visible leases, the full weekly report on all five, portfolio CSV + PDF exports, and the dossier-aware AI assistant. Premium — $99.95/mo is up to 10 visible leases plus the four things Essentials does not have: the monthly production report printed and mailed to you, three Lease Audits per term year on three leases (a Lease Audit is $500 on any plan, so that is $1,500 of value), extended history with advanced charts, and the private document vault. Enterprise is custom and contact-required. Annual prepay is exactly ten times the monthly price — two months free: Essentials $499.50/yr · Premium $999.50/yr.
Do paid plans auto-renew?
Never. Every paid plan is a 1-year term. We remind you before your end of term; if you do nothing, billing stops and your account moves to Free. Renewing is one click, and referral credits auto-apply at renewal.
Can I switch which owner record is my active one?
Yes. You can deactivate and switch your active owner once every 7 days (cooldown configurable). Enterprise supports custom multi-owner arrangements.
Who can see my private lease group?
Only claimed owners of that lease or unit, plus advisor representatives an owner explicitly brings in — always labeled "Advisor for [Owner]". Operators are never members of private lease groups.

Terms of Use

1. What Mineral View is (and is not)

Mineral View is an information service for mineral and royalty owners. We assemble public records, production data, activity, and model-based estimates so owners can understand what they own. Mineral View is not a broker: we do not buy or sell mineral rights, do not act as an intermediary in mineral transactions, and do not accept operator or buyer payments to influence what you see. Nothing on the service is legal, tax, investment, or appraisal advice.

2. Estimates — not appraisals

Every valuation on the service (including MVestimate) is a model-based estimate built from public records and stated assumptions. Estimates are labeled, forward-looking, and are not formal appraisals and not a payment ledger. Do not rely on them as the sole basis for selling, leasing, or litigating.

3. Your account and your claim

You may claim an owner record you have a good-faith basis to claim (yourself, a family member or entity you represent, or an estate you administer). Claiming on Mineral View does not change legal ownership of any mineral interest. You are responsible for the accuracy of what you submit and for keeping your credentials private.

4. Community rules

  1. Private lease groups are owners-only. Members are claimed owners of the lease; advisor representatives may participate only when an owner brings them in and are always labeled "Advisor for [Owner]." Operators are never members of private lease groups.
  2. No private data in public groups. Owner names, addresses, decimal interests, dollar amounts, and documents are auto-flagged in public groups.
  3. No cold solicitation. Groups are not a place to buy minerals or push offer letters. Violations remove the account.
  4. AI safety. The assistant never repeats private dossier data in a public reply — even at an owner's request.

5. Owner-first commitments

  • Mineral View does not sell owner personal data — not sold, brokered, or bundled to third parties.
  • Mineral View does not use private lease-group content or private documents to train AI models.
  • Mineral View does not act as a broker or intermediary in mineral transactions.
  • Mineral View does not condition premium features on data sharing with third-party buyers.

6. Acceptable use & termination

Don't scrape the service, misrepresent ownership, harass members, or attempt to access another member's private data. We may suspend accounts that break these terms; you may request deletion of your account at any time from Settings.

7. The other governing documents

Your relationship with Mineral View is governed by this document together with the Privacy Policy (what we collect, retention, and what "never sold" means), the Subscription Terms (plans, the 1-year term, no auto-renewal, downgrades), the Lease Audit Terms, and the Group Services Terms. Each carries its own version header; when you accept any of them, we record the document version and timestamp.

Subscription Terms

1. Plans and prices

Free is $0 forever (1 active owner · 1 visible lease). Paid plans: Essentials $49.95/mo (1 active owner · up to 5 visible leases), Premium $99.95/mo (1 active owner · up to 10 visible leases), Enterprise by contact only. Prices are in U.S. dollars, exclusive of taxes shown at checkout.

2. The 1-year term

Every paid subscription is a 1-year committed term. Your term starts at checkout completion and ends on the same calendar date one year later. At checkout you choose one of two ways to pay the term:

  1. Monthly billing within the term — twelve monthly charges ($49.95 Essentials / $99.95 Premium) across the 12-month term.
  2. Annual prepayment — pay once for the year. One payment of $499.50/yr (Essentials) or $999.50/yr (Premium) — exactly ten times the monthly price, so two months free versus monthly billing. Nothing more is charged during the term.

3. No auto-renewal — renewal is always explicit

Paid plans do not auto-renew into a new term. We send reminder emails before your end of term. If you take no action, billing stops at end of term and your account reverts to Free. Renewal is an explicit, one-click action in Billing — never a surprise charge. Referral credits auto-apply to the renewal amount.

4. Upgrades — immediate and prorated

Upgrades take effect immediately. You are billed only the prorated difference between plans through your existing end of term — or you may elect to restart a fresh 1-year term at the new plan's price.

5. Downgrades and cancellation — the term runs to its end

There are no mid-term downgrades and no mid-term cancellation refunds: a request to downgrade or cancel takes effect at the end of your current term, and your current plan and all its features continue until then. At end of term the account reverts to Free; leases beyond the Free limit are archived — never deleted — you choose which lease stays visible, private lease groups become read-only, and archived leases are fully restored if you re-subscribe. Payments are non-refundable except where required by law or where Mineral View is at fault (e.g. a duplicate charge); billing reviews disputes in good faith.

6. Referral credit — paid conversion only

Monthly billing and annual prepay both qualify — never a single month alone, and no credit is earned for a free signup. Credits cannot be transferred or redeemed for money, and are never paid for pressuring anyone to sell minerals.

7. Payment processing

Payments are processed by Braintree, a PayPal service. Mineral View never stores full card numbers. Taxes are calculated from your billing location and shown before you confirm.

8. Price changes

Mineral View may adjust prices, features, or lease-visibility limits with at least 30 days' notice before your next renewal. Your active term is never affected mid-flight.

9. Services governed by their own documents

The Mineral View Lease Audit is $500 per audit on any plan; a 12-month Premium term includes three per term year, on three leases. It is governed by the Lease Audit Terms. Group-hired professional services are governed by the Group Services Terms. Both documents carry their own version headers and acceptance records.

Lease Audit Terms

1. What the audit is — and is not

The Lease Audit compares the public production record to the statements you provide and flags possible discrepancies worth verifying. Findings are informational signals — the audit is not a certified audit, not a payment ledger, not a determination of underpayment, and not legal, tax, accounting, or investment advice. Whether any flagged month is a reporting, timing, deduction, or payment issue can only be settled by verification against your documents — and, where you choose, by a professional you engage.

2. Packaging and price

A 12-month Premium term — whether billed monthly within the term or prepaid annually — includes one Lease Audit per term year at no additional charge (not limited to the plan's visible leases). The included audit does not automatically renew with the term and is not an annual entitlement. Additional audits are $250 per lease, payable by card, PayPal, or referral credits. A $500 one-time portfolio analysis (all leases audited once, no subscription) is available as an alternative and does not auto-renew.

3. Your documents — analyzed, not stored

Uploaded statements are read for their facts and the files are then discarded; Mineral View retains the findings, never the documents. You may delete your audit findings at any time. Retention detail lives in the Privacy Policy retention schedule.

Group Services Terms

1. One all-in price

When a group hires a professional through Mineral View, the quoted price is the complete, all-in cost of the engagement — vetting and coordination included; no separate platform or service fee is added or itemized. The group's cost split (proportional by interest, or even, as the group elects) applies to that all-in total. Your card is authorised at pledge time but not charged. It is charged only when the group goal is met; if the goal is not met the authorisation is released and nothing is taken.

2. Mineral View's role — coordination, not opinions

Mineral View coordinates and vets group-hired engagements. Mineral View does not render legal, accounting, or audit opinions, and is not a party to the professional's conclusions. The professional's own engagement letter governs the work — who the professional is, what standards apply, and what the deliverable means. Read it before pledging.

3. Pledges and records

Each pledge is an explicit acceptance recorded with the service scope, the professional's identity, the all-in price, the split rule, the payment terms, and this document's version. Refunds follow the payment terms: goal not met → automatic refund.

4. Who may pledge — and why a claim is required

Group services are offered only inside a private lease group, and only claimed owners of record on that lease may pledge. Reading and posting in public groups requires no claim and confers no right to pledge. This is not a commercial gate: an engagement is priced and split against a specific set of owners on a specific lease, and an unverified participant would make both the split and the deliverable meaningless. Claiming is free and does not change legal ownership.

5. What co-owners can and cannot see

Your decimal interest is visible only to you. Other members of the group see aggregates — for example "3 owners pledged · 25% of participating interest" — never another owner's decimal, dollar figures, or documents, unless every affected owner consents on the confirmation screen. Your share is recomputed among the owners who actually elect in and is confirmed to the cent before any charge. Advisors appear only when an owner brings them in and are always labeled. Operators are never members of a private lease group.

6. Inviting co-owners

Invitations are generated for you but sent by you: Mineral View prints a personal letter and a single-use code for each owner of record you select, and does not mail on your behalf. Codes are single-use and expire unclaimed after twelve months. Adding co-owners lowers each participant's share of any group engagement; a referral credit, where offered, posts only on a referred owner's paid conversion after the confirmation window, never at free signup, and is never mentioned in the recipient's letter. Receiving a letter joins nobody to anything: each recipient claims their own record or does not, and Mineral View never creates an account on another person's behalf.

7. Community integrity — who is real, and what a count means

Mineral View does not create member accounts, posts, or member counts. No fabricated persona, no account operated on behalf of a fictitious owner, and no invented membership or activity total appears in any group, public or private. The only Mineral View presence in a group is a single account clearly labelled “MView — Official Account”, carrying the Mineral View logo, which posts platform content — permits, activity, price movements, explanatory material — and moderates. It is identified as official wherever it appears and is never presented as a mineral owner.

Two different numbers may be shown about a group and they are always labelled apart. Owners of record is a count of the interests recorded on the relevant county appraisal roll for that lease, county, operator or play; it describes the population a group serves and does not imply that those people are members. Members is a count of accounts that have actually joined, and is published only once it reflects real accounts. A group is not created for a lease with a single owner of record. Where a figure is illustrative rather than measured, it is marked as such on the page it appears on.

The full policy

1. What we collect

  • Account information — name, email, mailing address.
  • Lease and ownership information you enter, claim, or upload.
  • Usage data — pages viewed, alerts opened, features used.
  • Public records we retrieve and match on your behalf.

2. What we never do

  • Sell your personal data.
  • Share private lease-group content with third parties.
  • Send buyer solicitations on behalf of purchasers.
  • Use private lease content or your documents to train third-party AI models.

3. What "your data is never sold" means — exactly

The promise is absolute where it matters: no sale, no brokerage, no bundling, and no buyer or operator targeting — your name, address, decimal interests, dollar figures, documents, and group activity are never sold to, shared with, or used to build products for mineral buyers, operators, or data brokers.

What it does not mean: Mineral View runs on ordinary service providers — payment processing (Braintree, a PayPal service), hosting, analytics, email delivery, and security monitoring. These processors handle data only under contract, only to run the service for us, and are prohibited from using it for their own sales, marketing, or brokerage purposes. And like every company, we comply with valid legal process (subpoenas, court orders) — we will tell you when the law allows us to. Private documents and private group content are never used to train AI models.

4. How we use data

To deliver the service (dashboards, reports, alerts, groups), improve accuracy and stability, communicate about your account, and meet legal and security obligations. Public records are public; what you upload — division orders, check statements, deeds, photos — stays in your private vault unless you explicitly share it with an advisor, and you can revoke advisor sharing anytime.

AI assistant summariesSession-scoped; saved only if you save themDelete saved summaries anytimeNone
Invoices & receiptsAccount lifeCopy on request; originals retainedKept as tax/billing records even after account deletion
Audit logs (logins, consents, acceptances)Account life + statutory periodExport on request; not deletableKept as legal evidence of what you accepted
Group postsLife of the groupDelete your own posts anytime; quotes by others may remainModeration/safety holds
Support tickets3 yearsRequest redaction of personal contentOpen disputes held until resolved

Account deletion removes your claim, vault, findings, preferences, and group memberships. What survives — and why — is exactly the two bolded rows above: invoices (tax records) and the consent/audit log (proof of what was agreed). A legal hold can pause deletion; we notify you when the law allows.

6. Your rights

Access, correct, export, or delete your data anytime. Turning off marketing email never affects service email. Privacy requests: help@mineralview.com.

⚖
Two honest numbers, on purpose. Our estimate is a forward market cash-flow projection; the county's is a conservative annual tax value that lags about a year. Across 3.67 million Texas leases we run about 1.9× the county median — a methodology difference, not an error (the gap ranges from 0.77× to 10× by county, so no single correction factor would be honest). Policy: we show both and flag big gaps — we never quietly rescale your MVestimate. Gaps of roughly 3× or more get a Worth a look flag. To be clear: this flag is not a warning about your money. It usually means our forward projection sees more value than the county's lagging tax roll — potential upside worth understanding — not an error and not something wrong with your lease. Why a range, on this lease in particular. Ledbetter is oil-weighted, and nobody is paid the headline oil price. What your barrel sells for is WTI minus a discount that depends on the crude's gravity and sulphur and on where the pipeline out of Cass County takes it — a heavier, sourer barrel can fetch a couple of dollars less than a light sweet one produced a few miles away. On top of that we hold WTI flat at $68.78 for the whole window, and Caddo Pine's gathering and treating deducts are invisible to us until you show us a statement — your audited months already show deductions running 2.6% of gross against a ~1.8% area norm, which is exactly the kind of thing that moves the real cheque off our midpoint.

How the estimate is built →

Give us your division order and your last five cheques on this lease and we fit our model against what you were actually paid, then carry that correction forward and tell you how big it was. We are not claiming an accuracy figure today — that number only exists once your own statements are in, and it is computed from your record alone.

Explain this estimate — how the $5,300 is computed
The lease's cash-flow curve (fitted to the public RRC record since Aug 2019, peak $720k in Dec 2019) is projected six years forward at the current price outlook, then multiplied by your decimal interest 0.00243700. Gross $2,900,000 × 0.00243700 ≈ $5,300. Refreshes as production posts and prices move. A projection — not an appraisal, not a payment ledger, not advice.

The rock this lease drinks from

The Ledbetter lease produces from one underground layer of rock. That rock still holds about 38,000 barrels of oil and 39,000 units of gas expected to be produced over the next six years — your share of the money comes from that.

About this reservoir — in plain English

Narrative — descriptive, not data

What it is: the Lake Marlow field produces from the Upper Pettit, a limestone layer laid down in a shallow sea, deep beneath Cass County in the state's far northeast corner.

Read more — the history of this rock, and why it matters to you

It sits in East Texas's oldest oil country — fields around here have produced since the 1930s East Texas boom — but this lease is a modern take: a 2019 horizontal well that runs sideways through the pay zone instead of just poking through it, tagged to the Haynesville/Bossier play that made this corner of Texas busy again after 2008.

Why it matters to you: old, well-mapped rock plus a modern horizontal well is the friendly combination — the geology holds few surprises, so the decline curve (and your $5,300 share) is about the well slowly emptying a known tank, not about wondering what's down there. The neighbors drilling around Ledbetter are chasing the same understood rock, which is what keeps your acreage relevant.

A short orientation, not a geological report — the numbers live in the tables on this tab.

Ranges, not points — a gas unit's cheque depends on gas richness, flaring and deducts we can't see in advance.

Why a range, on a gas unit in particular. Gas is paid on more than the headline. We hold Henry Hub flat at $3.245 for the whole window, but what a unit actually earns depends on how rich its gas is — liquids-heavy gas can be worth several dollars an mcf more than dry gas — and on the area: some corners of Texas still flare associated gas and earn nothing for it at all. Then gathering, compression and treating come off before the cheque; your audited months put Bluestem's at 2.55% of gross against a ~2.4% area norm, close to typical but not something we can see in advance.

Give us your division order and your last five cheques on this unit and we fit our model against what you were actually paid, then carry that correction forward and tell you how big it was. We are not claiming an accuracy figure today — that number only exists once your own statements are in.

The rock this unit drinks from

This unit produces natural gas from a rock layer called the Wilcox. Most of its gas has already been produced, but about 290,000 units of gas are still expected over the next six years — that's where your $8,700 comes from.

About this reservoir — in plain English

Narrative — descriptive, not data

What it is: the Wilcox is a thick stack of ancient river-delta sands laid down when the Gulf Coast was building itself seaward, tens of millions of years ago. Under Bee County it sits deep and gas-charged.

Read more — the history of this rock, and why it matters to you

The "Massive E" in the field name is the driller's label for one of those stacked sand bodies. Wilcox sands are workhorse Gulf Coast producers: not flashy, but they flow for decades, which is exactly what this unit has done since Chevron drilled it in 2003.

Why it matters to you: a 20-year-plus Wilcox gas tail is the steady-eddy kind of minerals ownership — long, shallow decline, few surprises, income that shows up as long as the well is kept open. The risk to watch isn't the rock running out suddenly; it's the operator deciding the tail is no longer worth maintaining. That's why the operator card and your Activities feed matter as much as the geology here.

A short orientation, not a geological report — the numbers live in the tables on this tab. The formal play classification for this field is not classified in the state's play table (a confirmed source gap, not a data error) — we say so rather than invent one.

Why we give a band and not a figure. We hold today's prices flat for the whole window, the discount off the benchmark varies with oil quality and with the area a lease sits in, gathering and compression deducts differ lease by lease and we cannot see yours, and operators post production two to three months behind. A single number would look more useful and be less true.

What the 228 new-production activity records are — and what they mean for you

What they are: each record is one "New Production" activity row in the state's feed — one month's production filed on one of your leases or a lease adjacent to them: "we produced this much oil and gas here this month." Your 10 leases plus the 22 adjacent ones is how the neighborhood adds up to 228.

What they mean for you: posting production means the lease reported production — your payment still depends on your decimal, statement timing, deductions, and operator remittance. Records on your leases feed the estimate model and the decline curve behind your MVestimate; records on the adjacent leases tell you the neighborhood is still working. And what it costs, plainly. Premium is $99.95 a month — about $23 a week, or about $19 a week on the annual plan ($999.50). What we will not do is tell you what that watch has "saved" you. Production is public and payment is not: the only place an underpayment can be proven is on your own statements, which is exactly what the Lease Audit included with your plan is for. What the subscription promises is narrower and testable — the watch runs every morning, a quiet week gets a quiet page, and nothing here was invented to look busy.

Professional note — how the watch is built. A daily 6:00 AM sweep of RRC production, permit, completion and status filings matched against your ten lease numbers and the 1-mile radius lists around them, plus the price feed, your private group threads, the decline model's band changes and the audit-findings store. Events are deduplicated across dashboard, alerts and email, so one filing never reaches you three times, and a repeat fires only when the underlying fact changes. Every alert carries both its event date and the date we detected it. History is kept 12 months. A week with nothing in it costs the same to produce as a week with nine — which is the difference between paying for a watch and paying for a feed.

$330

That's what your ten leases look set to pay you next month, before your operator's own deductions. We give a range because a single number would be a guess wearing a suit — prices move, and we can't see what comes off your cheque until we see one.

Why it's a range and not a number

  • We hold today's prices flat. The model runs WTI at $68.78 and Henry Hub at $3.245 for the whole month. Real prices don't hold still, and neither will your cheque.
  • The differential varies by oil quality and by area. Nobody is paid the benchmark. What your barrel actually sells for is the benchmark minus a discount that depends on gravity, sulphur and where the pipeline takes it — a heavier barrel can fetch a couple of dollars less than a light sweet one out of the same county. On gas it cuts the other way: rich, liquids-heavy gas can pay well above the headline, and in some areas the gas is flared and pays nothing at all.
  • Deducts are the part we genuinely cannot see. Gathering, compression, treating and marketing come off before your cheque and they differ lease by lease. Until you show us a statement, we are estimating them from area norms.
  • The calendar drifts. Operators post production two to three months behind, and the cheque month is not always the production month — a month can land in the next envelope.
  • Volumes can move. A workover, a shut-in, a cold snap or a pipeline outage moves a month either way, and the decline model only learns about it after the fact.
◳
What this is: a forward model of your own leases, sliced to next month. What it is not: a payment ledger, a promise, or an appraisal. If your statement lands outside this range, the model was wrong — not your operator, and not necessarily either.

Make this estimate more accurate

You keep the documents — we keep the maths

The widest part of that range is the part only your paperwork can close: your exact decimal, and what your operator actually takes out. Two things shrink it fast.

① Your division orders

They state your exact decimal interest on each lease. Right now we use the decimal on the public record; a division order replaces an assumption with a fact.

② Your last five monthly cheques

Statements show the real deducts and the real price you were paid — the two inputs we are currently estimating from area norms.

Or run your included Lease Audit →
What we'd do with five cheques — the honest version
We line up each month you were actually paid against what this model said that month would be, and fit the difference. If the model ran consistently high, we carry that correction forward, and the report starts telling you the size of it in plain words — the sentence takes the form "across your last five cheques we ran about X% high, so we've reduced the estimate by X% from here." We are not claiming a figure today: X only exists once your own statements are in, it is computed from your record and nobody else's, and it is re-fitted every time a new cheque lands. Five months is the minimum that makes the fit worth anything; more is better. Documents are analyzed, not stored.

Method, for the professional view: a per-owner ordinary-least-squares fit of remitted owner-share against modeled owner-share by production month, one fit per operator where the sample allows it (deduct structures are an operator/area property, not an owner property). The correction is applied as a multiplicative bias term to the central estimate; the band is re-derived from the residual spread rather than the fixed ±24% prior, so a well-fitted record gets a genuinely narrower range instead of a cosmetic one. Under five paired months the fit is not reported at all.

What this report is made of — four layers, and only two of them are free

Where the knowledge comes from

Two of the four layers under this report are public — hard to assemble, but public. The third we build ourselves: the decline curves, your estimate, the produced-versus-paid signal. The fourth — what a barrel out of your area really sells for, and what your operator really deducts — nobody has yet, and it is the reason next month is a range and not a number.

Layer 1 · The public record
Public, but not accessible
Texas publishes it all: 1,217,273 wells, 33,696 operators, 915,037 mineral-owner records across the 192 counties with owner data. Free to anyone — scattered across separate systems, keyed on numbers you don't have, and never joined to your name. The joining is the work.
Layer 2 · Findable if you go looking
Google has it. Nobody has the hour.
Prices, world events, what's drilling in your county, how your operator behaves. All of it is out there every week. The value isn't in owning it — it's in someone reading it against your three counties every Saturday and saying, in one line, whether it touched your number.
Layer 3 · What Mineral View builds
Derived, not looked up
Your decline curves and the six-year MVestimate, the produced-versus-paid signal on Ledbetter, the 1-mile radius lists (22 adjacent leases, 38 permits), the new-well probability band. None of this exists in a public database — it is computed, on your record, and it is most of what you're reading.
Layer 4 · The one nobody has Not built yet
Lease-to-lease economics
What a barrel out of your area actually sells for after its differential; whether the gas on your unit is rich enough that the liquids pay well above the headline, or flared and paying nothing; what your operator genuinely deducts. It is owner-held knowledge and it does not exist in any record — it only comes into being when owners pool their own statements.

Why we're telling you this. Layer 4 is the honest reason your August estimate is $330 – $540 and not a single figure — the widest part of that band is the part only paperwork can close. It is also the only layer you can help build: your division orders and last five cheques narrow your own range first, and your private lease group is where owners of the same unit compare the same month. We are not claiming to have layer 4 today. We're telling you what it would be worth and what it is going to take.

Professional note. The layers are a build order as much as a value ladder. Layers 1 and 2 are ingest and editorial — commodity work with a real assembly cost and no defensibility. Layer 3 is the current product surface and is defensible only for as long as the modelling stays ahead. Layer 4 is the only layer with a compounding moat, because its input is owner-contributed and its accuracy improves per statement rather than per engineer: a per-operator, per-area regression of remitted owner-share against modeled owner-share needs paired months from many owners on many leases, and every owner who uploads makes the estimate better for every other owner on that operator. That is why the statement upload is framed as a benefit to the owner rather than a data request — it has to be true for the owner first, or it never gets the volume it needs.

Glossary corner

Decimal interest
Your ownership share of a lease, written as a decimal — e.g. 0.00538700 on Smith 305892. Multiply gross lease dollars by it to get your share.
MVestimate
Your projected six-year owner-share earnings at the current decline and price outlook. Forward-looking — an estimate, never an appraisal.
Reservoir
The underground rock layer a lease produces from. One lease → one reservoir → possibly several wells.
EUR — estimated ultimate recovery
Everything a lease (or a single well) is expected to produce over its whole life. EUR − produced = what's left (reserves).

That's your week

Earning as expected, nothing on your land, one thing worth a few minutes when you have them. If you do only one thing after closing this: run the Lease Audit that comes with your plan on Ledbetter — it is the single question this week raised that only your own paperwork can answer. Otherwise, nothing needs you. We'll be back on Saturday, and if the week is quiet we'll say that too.

What we'd do with this week, if the record were ours

  1. Settle Ledbetter. Three produced gas months are visible in the public record and we cannot see a single payment. That is not an accusation — it is the one open question on the whole record, and the audit included with your plan closes it either way. An answer of "you were paid correctly" is worth having.
  2. Leave the two quiet Smith units alone, but keep watching them. 267145 and 508936 post real volumes — 58,580 and 26,220 mcf — and project nothing to your decimal. Nothing to do about that this week. If a recompletion is ever filed on either, that is the largest upside on this record and it will arrive as an alert before it arrives as money.
  3. Do nothing about the price. Gas firmed 1.53% and your estimate held. Weeks like this are the argument for not re-reading your minerals every time a headline moves — the six-year figure is built on the boring average, and it should not twitch.
  4. If an offer letter arrives, read it against page 5 before you answer it. Eleven permits within a mile of Ledbetter is exactly the kind of activity that puts letters in mailboxes. An offer is only judgeable against a number you already had.

What would change our mind

A forecast that cannot be wrong in a stated way is not a forecast. These are this issue's falsification conditions — the observations that would force a revision rather than a footnote.

  • A statement outside the band. August lands below $330 or above $540 and the model — not the operator — is the thing that failed. Two consecutive misses in the same direction is a bias, not noise, and re-fits the record.
  • A drift beyond ~2σ on any lease. This month's largest was +2.4% on Smith 267145, well inside the curve's own noise. A single lease past two standard deviations of its expected month raises the inflection alert and the decline parameters get re-estimated before the next issue.
  • A structural price break. Gas sustained above ~$4 or oil back over $100 re-rates the MVestimate portfolio-wide; a slide toward COVID-era prices does the reverse. Both lead the report when they happen — neither is treated as news at a single day's close.
  • Any paired statement month. The band on this record is a ±24% prior, not a measured error — it is what we use because we have measured nothing on this owner yet. The first five paired months replace it with a residual spread, and if that spread is wider than the prior, the range gets wider, published as such.
  • A deduct schedule we can see. Layer 4, above. The differential and the deducts are currently estimated from area norms; one real statement replaces an assumption on this record, and enough of them across an operator replaces it for everyone on that operator.

None of the above is a prediction that it will happen. It is the list of things that would make this issue's numbers wrong, published in the issue itself, because a report you are meant to hand to an adviser has to name its own failure modes.

The two units in that table, in plain English. bbl is a barrel of oil — 42 gallons. mcf is a thousand cubic feet of gas, roughly what an average home burns in four days. Why an owner should care about a group at all

The honest answer

A mineral owner is usually alone: one statement, no way to check it, no leverage with the operator, and no budget for a professional. A group fixes all four of those — not by being a nice place to chat, but arithmetically.

◉ Find out if you're being paid like everyone else

Your statement on its own tells you nothing — there is no number to compare it to. Owners on the same lease, same month, same volumes, comparing what they were actually paid: that is the only comparison that exists. It is how underpayment gets found.

◆ Face the operator as a group

A question from one owner with half a percent gets a form letter. The same question signed by twelve owners of the same unit gets an answer. Groups can ask for things an individual simply cannot — a recompletion plan, a deduction breakdown, a corrected division order.

✚ Hire professionals at a fraction of the cost

A royalty audit runs about $5,000. Nobody with an $8,700 interest buys that alone. Twelve owners split it to ≈$417 each; twenty owners to ≈$250. Same for an oil & gas attorney or a minerals CPA. Illustrative figures.

⌲ Share what you each already know

Permits next door, offer letters going around the county, how to read a deduction line, which operators post late. One owner sees a sliver of it. A room full of owners sees the pattern.

◆
The short version: an owner with half a percent will never pay for an accountant on their own. Fifty of them together will — and that is the entire point of the room.

Why this rung matters — before you get to it

Inviting co-owners is not a favour to Mineral View. It is the step that turns a claimed record into representation: a group that can compare payments line by line, put one question to the operator with twelve names under it, and afford a professional none of you would buy alone. Everything on this page exists for that, and nothing else on it works until it happens.

The co-owners are already there. 78.9% of Texas leases carry more than one owner of record — a median of 24. You are not recruiting strangers; you are telling the people who already legally co-own these minerals with you where the records are. Appraisal rolls · measured 24 Jul 2026

Why would you mail twenty letters?

The reason, plainly

Because one owner is not a party to anything. On your own you are a small decimal with no way to check what you were paid, no answer worth waiting for from the operator, and no realistic budget for a professional. Twenty of you is a different kind of thing entirely: a group that can compare payments line by line, put one question to the operator with twenty names under it, and hire the accountant none of you could afford alone. That group does not exist until somebody writes to it — and the only person who can is you. Mineral View cannot invite them on your behalf; a letter from a name they recognise gets opened, and a letter from a company they have never heard of does not.

The twenty already exist, which is the part most owners do not realise. They are on the same county appraisal roll you are, they own the same unit, and they are in the same position — most of them have never seen a second owner's statement either. 78.9% of Texas leases carry more than one owner of record, a median of 24 each. You are not recruiting strangers into something. You are telling the people who already legally co-own these minerals with you where the records are. Appraisal rolls · measured 24 Jul 2026

◆ Every letter divides the cost of everything

A royalty audit on this lease is $5,000. At 12 co-owners that's $417 each. At 20 it's $250. Same for an attorney review or a minerals CPA. Each letter you send makes every future decision cheaper for you personally — not just for them. Illustrative split.

◉ Twenty names get answered. One doesn't.

A question from one owner with half a percent gets a form letter. The same question signed by the owners of the whole unit gets a real answer — a deduction breakdown, a recompletion plan, a corrected division order. Representation is a headcount, and right now yours is one.

⌲ They hold the half of the record you can't see

Your statement can't be checked against itself. Theirs covers the same wells, the same months, a different decimal. Put the two side by side and a payment gap becomes visible — that comparison does not exist until a second owner is in the room.

✚ The family stops depending on one person's memory

Most mineral families run on whoever kept the folder. Once co-owners are claimed, everyone sees the same map, the same production and the same activity — through an estate, a sale, or an inheritance nobody planned for. And if an invited co-owner later goes paid, a $100 credit posts to you.

◆
What it actually costs you: Mineral View prints the letters, the codes and the QR sheets. You address them and buy stamps — about twelve dollars for twenty. Against a $5,000 audit that drops to $250 a head once they are in, that is the cheapest thing on this page. The people you're writing to already legally co-own these minerals with you: you are not selling them anything, and the letter never mentions your credit.

And what it does not do: nobody is added to anything by receiving a letter. Each person claims their own record or doesn't. Mineral View never creates an account on someone's behalf, and never counts an uninvited owner as a member — a group's size is the real people in it plus the real owners of record on the roll, and those two numbers are always shown apart (decision D-005).

Mineral View Lease Audit

Free account — you haven't claimed your owner record yet.

Is your operator paying you correctly? Nobody has ever checked.

Your operator measures the production, sets the price, takes the deductions, applies your decimal and mails you a check. There is no referee. A Mineral View Lease Audit is that check: we take the public production record for your wells, work out what your share of each month should have come to, and line it up against the stubs you were actually paid. Anything that doesn't line up is flagged in plain English — as a question worth asking, never an accusation.

It starts with your claim. The math has to know which leases are yours and what decimal you own — so a claimed record comes first. Claiming is free.

Claim your record — free

Nothing on this page is a finding about your payments — we have never seen your statements. When you do send them they are analyzed, not stored: files are discarded at audit completion unless you choose "Save to Vault." We keep the findings, never the documents. Proposed policy — final wording lands with the service contract.

Services

Mineral View Lease Audit

Do your production and payments line up? A Mineral View Lease Audit compares the two — from your statements and the real production data — and flags what's worth verifying.

3 audits a year included with your Premium plan $500 each · Premium includes 3 a year Informational — not legal, tax, or investment advice

Lease Audit — are you being paid correctly?

Findings say "worth verifying" — never an accusation

We check that the money you were paid matches the oil and gas your land produced — and tell you in plain words if it doesn't.

Your operator works out your check. Nobody checks their math. An audit lines up two things that have never been compared: what the public record says your wells produced, and what your own check stubs say you were paid.

You send your division order and your stubs — phone photos are fine. We do the arithmetic for every month and hand you a plain-English report. Plenty of audits come back clean, and that is a real answer too. Knowing beats hoping.

Why it exists. The royalty owner is the only party in the chain who cannot check the arithmetic. The operator measures the volumes, sets the price, applies the deductions, applies your decimal, and mails the result — and an owner holding a fraction of a percent will never hire an accountant to verify a $180 check. So in practice nobody verifies it, ever. Errors here are rarely dramatic; they are small, and they repeat in every check for years. Mineral View is not a broker and does not buy minerals: we are not against selling, we are against deciding anything blind. The audit exists so that "am I being paid correctly?" finally has an answer.

How it's done. ① You send your division order and as many check stubs as you have. ② We read them and show you every value we extracted, so you confirm it — we never quietly assume a number. ③ We pull the public production record for those exact leases and months and re-compute what each month should have paid: production × the price on your stub × your decimal interest, less severance tax. ④ You get a report in plain English: expected against paid, month by month, with anything off flagged and explained.

What we check
  • Volumes — did every barrel and mcf posted to the public record show up on a check? operator-reported postings vs your stubs
  • Prices — is the price on your stub in the normal range for that month? your stub vs the published index — a reasonableness check, not a rule
  • Your interest — does the decimal on your stub match your division order? to all 8 decimals
  • Deductions — are processing and gathering charges consistent with your lease? flagged "verify" whenever the lease is silent or you don't have it
  • Missing months — production posted with no matching payment line the most common flag — often timing, suspense, or a minimum-check threshold; always "verify," never "unpaid" as fact
What we don't do
  • We don't verify title or heirship who legally owns what is a records and attorney question
  • We don't interpret your lease's legal language ambiguous clauses are flagged "verify," never ruled on
  • We don't contact your operator or file claims for you the findings are yours — what you do with them is your call
  • We don't issue a certified audit findings are "possible discrepancies worth verifying," not legal, tax, or accounting determinations
  • We never buy your minerals, or take a cut of anything you recover Mineral View is not a broker — the audit is the product, your minerals are not

The method, in fullProfessional view
Expected, per lease-monthRRC posted volume × stub realized price × DI − severance tax
Production sourceRRC lease-level monthly postings (oil bbl · gas mcf), joined on lease number
Interest sourceyour division order decimal to 8 places — never the decimal printed on the stub being tested
Price handlingyour stub's realized price drives the math; the published index is a band check only (differentials are normal)
Deduction adjudicationlease clause governs where supplied; otherwise every deduction is flagged unadjudicated
Known confoundersprior-period adjustments, suspense, minimum-check thresholds, unit re-allocations, take-in-kind
Confidence tiershigh on volume and DI joins · moderate on deductions without a lease · informational on price
Out of scopetitle, heirship, certified opinion, operator correspondence, claim filing

Conservative by construction: a variance is reported as a possible discrepancy to verify, with its source shown, and is never characterised as an error, an underpayment, or misconduct. The problem nobody checks

The royalty owner is the only party in the chain who cannot check the arithmetic. The operator measures the volumes, sets the price, applies the deductions, applies your decimal, and mails the result. Operators cut thousands of royalty checks a month and honest mistakes happen: possible decimal mismatches, deduction questions the lease language would settle, payment-month gaps, price differences worth checking. Nobody ever compares — so open questions quietly ride along for years, in every check.

You all share the same lease and the same operator. If a discrepancy exists at the lease level, co-owners may want to verify the same issue together — your brothers, cousins, and the co-owners you've never met would see it in the same months.

Mineral View Lease Audit

Your operator works out your check. Nobody checks their math.

A Lease Audit is that check. The operator measures the production, sets the price, takes the deductions, applies your decimal and mails you a check — and the royalty owner is the only party in the chain who cannot verify any of it. Public records show what was produced. Only your statements show what was paid. We compare the two, month by month, and flag what's worth verifying — in plain English, as a question worth asking, never an accusation.

An owner with a fraction of a percent will never hire an accountant to verify a $180 check, so in practice nobody ever does. Errors here are rarely dramatic — they are small, and they repeat in every check for years. Mineral View is not a broker and never buys minerals: we are not against selling, we are against deciding anything blind. The audit exists so that "am I being paid correctly?" finally has an answer.

1 · You send two documents

Your division order — the one-pager with your ownership decimal — and your check stubs, as many months as you have. Phone photos are fine. Your lease helps but is optional.

2 · You confirm what we read

We show you every value we extracted — your decimal to eight places, each month's volumes, prices and deductions — and you confirm it. Nothing is quietly assumed.

3 · We re-compute every month

Public production record × the price on your stub × your decimal, less severance tax — against what you were actually paid. Index prices are a reasonableness check only.

4 · You get a plain-English report

Expected vs paid, month by month, every flag explained with its source shown — and a PDF you can hand to your operator, your co-owners, or a professional. What you do with it is always your call.

What we check

  • Volumes — did every barrel and mcf posted publicly show up on a check?
  • Prices — is the price on your stub in the normal range for that month?
  • Your interest — does the decimal on your stub match your division order, to all 8 places?
  • Deductions — are processing and gathering charges consistent with your lease?
  • Missing months — production posted with no matching payment line often timing, suspense, or a minimum-check threshold — always "verify," never "unpaid" as fact

What we don't do

  • We don't verify title or heirship who legally owns what is a records and attorney question
  • We don't interpret your lease's legal language ambiguous clauses are flagged "verify," never ruled on
  • We don't contact your operator or file claims for you
  • We don't issue a certified audit findings are possible discrepancies worth verifying — not legal, tax, or accounting determinations
  • We never buy your minerals or take a cut of anything you recover

What an audit actually finds — a worked example

Illustrative example — not cohort data

An illustrative audit re-computes 14 months of statements on an oil-and-gas lease against the public production record. In this example it flags: 3 produced months where the sample statements show no matching gas payment line, deductions running above the area norm, and one short oil month — $137.94 as a modeled amount to verify, laid out month by month in a table the owner can check in minutes.

Honest math: many audits come back clean — that's the peace of mind. We don't yet have recovery statistics to quote — any figures here are illustrative — we have no cohort data yet. What we can say without inventing anything: an audit is $500, Premium includes three a year, and a statement issue you verify once stops repeating in every future check. Because errors compound, the earlier you check, the more a catch is worth.
